documentation.range: The Frilled Shark has a widespread, yet patchy, distribution in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans (Ebert et al. 2021).
documentation.population: No data are available on population size, trends, and structure of the Frilled Shark. Global population trend is suspected to be stable based on refuge at depth from fishing effort in parts of its range.
documentation.habitats: The Frilled Shark is epibenthic, pelagic, and demersal on offshore shelves and upper continental and island slopes at depths of 17−1,520 m (Ebert et al. 2021). It reaches a maximum size of 196 cm total length (TL). Size at maturity is ~118 cm total length (TL) for males, 126−150 cm TL for females, and size at birth is ~39−60 cm TL (Ebert et al. 2021). Reproduction is viviparous with litter sizes of 2−15 pups per litter and a gestation period of 1−3 years (Ebert et al. 2021).
documentation.threats: The Frilled Shark is infrequently taken as bycatch in demersal and midwater trawl, longline, and gillnet fisheries across most of its range (e.g., Neat et al. 2015, Delgado et al. 2017, Kyne et al. 2021). There are a few known regions where the species has been more frequently recorded, including off Japan and New Zealand (Kubota et al. 1991, B. Finucci, unpub. data). A single trawl off the mid-Atlantic Ridge to the north of the Azores recorded 34 Frilled Sharks in 2003 and it was suspected that this trawl took place during a mating event (Kukueva and Pavlov 2008). Any expansion of fisheries into deeper waters or previously unexploited areas where the Frilled Shark is known to occur should be closely monitored.
documentation.measures: There are some national and regional initiatives aimed at reducing bycatch of deepwater sharks which benefit the Frilled Shark. For example, in the Northeast Atlantic Ocean, the North East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC) banned targeted fishing for deepwater sharks, including Frilled Shark; restricted the expansion of the fishing footprint by designating existing fishing areas where bottom fishing is permitted; and has closed extensive areas to protect vulnerable marine ecosystems (VMEs) (ICES 2023). In the Southwest Pacific Ocean, most areas below 700 m are closed to trawling in the Commonwealth Trawl Sector of the Australian Southern and Eastern Scalefish and Shark Fishery (Patterson et al. 2022), providing refuge at depth for this species. Further research is needed on population size and trends, and life history, and catch rates should be monitored.
documentation.use_trade: The Frilled Shark is utilized for fishmeal and meat, and is occasionally kept in aquaria in Japan (Higashi et al. 2015, Yamada et al. 2019).
documentation.rationale: The Frilled Shark (Chlamydoselachus anguineus) is a medium-sized (to 196 cm total length) deepwater shark with a widespread, yet patchy, distribution in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. It is epibenthic, pelagic, and demersal on offshore shelves and upper continental and island slopes at depths of 17−1,520 m. No data are available on population size, trends, and structure. The Frilled Shark is infrequently taken as bycatch in demersal and midwater trawl, longline, and gillnet fisheries across most of its range although there are a few known locations where the species has been more frequently recorded, including off Japan and New Zealand. There are some national and regional management actions that will benefit the Frilled Shark, including the prohibition of targeted fishing for deepwater shark in some regions and areas closed to fishing activities. Thus, the species has significant refuge at depth in these regions and also in many parts of its range where fisheries do not operate to its maximum depth. Any expansion of fisheries into deeper waters or previously unexploited areas where the Frilled Shark is known to occur should be closely monitored. At this time, there is nothing to infer or suspect population decline and the Frilled Shark is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The Southern African Frilled Shark Chlamydoselachus africana Ebert & Compagno, 2009 is distinct from C. anguineus.
